posts.title: Two decisions in Europe this month will shape how crypto exchanges operate there, and both matter to us because HUMB has MiCA applications in progress in Lithuania and Cyprus.
posts.author: Dr Richard Satur
posts.snippet:
Two decisions in Europe this month will shape how crypto exchanges operate there, and both matter to us because HUMB has MiCA applications in progress in Lithuania and Cyprus.

The first came on October 9, when EU finance ministers agreed their position on moving the largest crypto service providers under the direct supervision of ESMA, the EU’s securities markets regulator. Under MiCA today, a firm licensed in one member state can serve customers across the EU, and the regulator in its home country remains its main supervisor.

The Council’s position would change that only for the biggest firms, meaning those with at least 15 million active users in the EU, or those that meet three of five other measures of size, such as holding more than €1 billion in crypto assets for clients. Officials expect only 10 to 15 of the roughly 360 providers to qualify, and the proposal still has to be negotiated with the European Parliament before it becomes law.

For a specialist exchange, this means the home regulator will remain the supervisor that matters, and the application itself carries most of the weight. Part of the push for central oversight came from concern about how some firms were authorized, including a 2025 ESMA review that questioned how one national regulator had approved a provider. I expect national regulators to review new applications more carefully as a result, and I would rather go through a careful review now than build on a license that gets questioned later.

The second decision came a day earlier. On October 8, ESMA told national regulators that MiCA-authorized firms should stop offering services involving stablecoins that have not been authorized under MiCA, and should clear their clients’ existing holdings within three months, which points to early January 2027. ESMA’s reasoning is that a firm cannot act in its clients’ best interests while offering an asset whose issuer has not met the rules, and that warning clients does not change that. The opinion is guidance to supervisors, and it does not stop anyone from owning these tokens, but it does change what a regulated exchange can offer.

That reasoning applies well beyond stablecoins. An exchange is responsible for what it lists, and for a healthcare exchange, every token needs an issuer who can be identified and a legal position that has been checked before it reaches customers. Healthcare organizations already work under this kind of scrutiny in the rest of their business, so they will expect the same from any exchange they deal with.

posts.title: How trustworthy is the US Capital Market ?
posts.author: Volker Potthoff
posts.snippet:
How trustworthy is the US Capital Market ?

During my professional career in capital markets I was taught that the American capital market regulation is the global benchmark for transparency, investor protection and the rule of law. But can that reputation still be taken for granted?
Three developments raise serious questions about the integrity of the system.

👉The SEC: Is the market watchdog losing its independence?
A functioning capital market depends on an independent regulator that applies the rules equally — regardless of political connections, wealth or influence.
Yet recent developments raise concerns about the SEC’s enforcement priorities, particularly in crypto markets and politically sensitive cases.
•	Potentially informed trading ahead of government announcements: In March 2026, Reuters reported on unusually well-timed, profitable trades ahead of major Trump administration policy announcements involving tariffs, Venezuela and Iran. 
•	Political influence and crypto: President Trump’s family has substantial financial interests in crypto ventures, including $TRUMP and World Liberty Financial.
•	Enforcement priorities: Though legal experts called for investigations in particular in the areas of possible insider trading/front running as well as crypto I could  not notice any enforcement against members of the Trump family, the Trump administration or even Tech oligarchs.

👉Tech companies corporate governance look like autocratic structures
•	Elon Musk — Tesla and SpaceX: Musk’s influence across multiple companies and his political involvement raise questions about conflicts of interest, oversight and the alignment of management decisions with shareholder interests.
•	Mark Zuckerberg — Meta: Meta’s dual-class share structure gives Zuckerberg substantial voting control relative to ordinary shareholders. 
•	Sam Altman — OpenAI: The governance crisis that culminated in Altman’s temporary removal and rapid reinstatement in 2023. 
•	Alex Karp — Palantir: Palantir’s work with governments and security institutions places its leadership at the intersection of technology, state power and political decision-making. 

👉Political influence is becoming a capital-market risk
When corporate leaders can influence public policy, regulation, government contracts it avoids in my opinion fair competition and creates intransparancy topics investors usually hate as it affects the integrity of capital markets.
How do institutional investors evaluate this risk in particular affecting the Tech oligarchs? Please discuss!

posts.title: A client holding a stablecoin through a MiCA-authorised CASP may have to decide whether to sell it, convert it or move it elsewhere. Many did not expect to face that decision.
posts.author: Alessandro Negri della Torre
posts.snippet:
A client holding a stablecoin through a MiCA-authorised CASP may have to decide whether to sell it, convert it or move it elsewhere. Many did not expect to face that decision.

On 8 October ESMA issued an opinion to national authorities on crypto-asset services involving ARTs and EMTs that do not comply with MiCA. It is addressed to supervisors and is not legislation; national authorities will apply it.

📌 ESMA starts from Art. 66(1) MiCA, the duty to act in clients' best interests. It treats any MiCA service on a non-compliant token as presumptively incompatible with that duty. Warnings, disclosures and client acknowledgements are not considered sufficient.

Existing exposures should be remediated no later than three months after publication, which points to 8 January 2027. In the meantime, ESMA expects residual services to be limited to liquidation, conversion, withdrawal, transfer and safekeeping of existing holdings, for a limited time and clearly communicated to clients.

In my view the legal reading is fairly clear. What takes care is the message to each client: which services stop and how much time is left to decide. I would draft it before changing the product, with a named contact for questions.

If you are preparing that message, what are clients asking you first?

🇮🇹
Per chi detiene una stablecoin presso un CASP autorizzato, la scelta tra liquidare, convertire o trasferire può arrivare senza essere stata prevista.

L'opinione ESMA dell'8 ottobre, rivolta alle autorità nazionali, parte dall'art. 66, par. 1, MiCAR: offrire servizi su ART o EMT non conformi si presume incompatibile con il dovere di agire nel migliore interesse del cliente. Avvertenze e prese d'atto non bastano.

Le esposizioni esistenti vanno sistemate entro tre mesi dalla pubblicazione, quindi entro l'8 gennaio 2027. Nel frattempo, per l'ESMA, i servizi residui vanno limitati a liquidazione, conversione, prelievo, trasferimento e custodia.

A mio avviso la parte che richiede più cura è la comunicazione al cliente: quali servizi si fermano e quanto tempo resta per decidere. La scriverei prima di cambiare il prodotto, indicando una persona a cui rivolgersi.

Cosa vi chiedono per primi i clienti?

posts.title: Not every legal dispute can be resolved simply by reading statutory provisions. In some cases the issue is the correct interpretation of the applicable rules; in others the technic
posts.author: Cindemir Law Office
posts.snippet:
Not every legal dispute can be resolved simply by reading statutory provisions. In some cases the issue is the correct interpretation of the applicable rules; in others the technical, financial or digital background must first be clarified. Although the terms legal opinion and expert opinion are sometimes used interchangeably, they do not serve the same function.


A legal opinion is a structured assessment of how an event or relationship should be understood in light of legislation, case law and the facts: it is normative and asks what the legal meaning of what happened is. An expert opinion, regulated in Turkish civil procedure under Article 293 of the Code of Civil Procedure, explains matters requiring special or technical knowledge. It is not the same as a court-appointed expert report, and it does not replace legal analysis.


The distinction is particularly visible in crypto-asset, digital-platform and international-trade disputes, where legal characterisation (for example the nature of a token or the validity of an arbitration clause) is a different question from technical tracing, accounting records or platform architecture.

comments.text: This distinction matters a lot in token classification work too — whether something is a utility token, an e-money token or an asset-referenced token is a legal characterisation question, but the tokenomics modelling behind it is squarely technical and needs its own expert input rather than being folded into the legal opinion.

In crypto disputes specifically, do Turkish courts tend to accept expert reports on token architecture as sufficient on their own, or do they still expect a separate legal opinion on characterisation before weighing the technical findings?

We run into the same split constantly on token work — clients often expect a single opinion to cover both the legal classification and the technical tracing, when in practice those need to be kept analytically separate even if they end up in the same deliverable.

posts.title: Every year, RBI cancels the licences of NBFCs. Most people read it as a compliance footnote.
posts.author: Varun Sharma
posts.snippet:
Every year, RBI cancels the licences of NBFCs. Most people read it as a compliance footnote. 

I read it as a case study.

After years in this industry, I’ve noticed that licences are rarely lost overnight. They’re lost slowly, through decisions that looked harmless at the time. Here are the patterns I keep seeing:

1. Growth outran governance
Disbursements doubled, but risk, audit and compliance teams stayed the same size. When the book grows faster than your controls, you’re borrowing against your licence.

2. Net Owned Fund (NOF) was treated as a one-time hurdle
Meeting the minimum NOF requirement at registration is easy. Maintaining it through losses, write-offs and aggressive expansion is what separates survivors from casualties.

3. Reporting wasn’t taken seriously
Late returns, mismatched data and inconsistent disclosures are early warning signs. Regulators read patterns, not just numbers.

4. Funding was concentrated and fragile
Too much reliance on a few lenders or short-term borrowings against long-term assets. When liquidity tightens, ALM mismatches become existential.

5. Fair Practices Code was a document, not a culture
Opaque charges, aggressive recovery and weak grievance redressal eventually reach the regulator. In lending, customer conduct is a licence issue.

6. Outsourcing without accountability
Digital lending partners, collection agencies and LSPs can’t be someone else’s problem. RBI holds the NBFC responsible, always.

7. Promoters mixed personal and company interests
Related-party exposures and weak board independence have ended more NBFCs than bad loans have.

8. Dormancy and silence
Many licences are cancelled simply because the entity stopped operating or stopped responding. Regulatory silence is never neutral.

The takeaway: a licence is not an asset you own. It’s a trust you renew every single day, through capital discipline, clean data, ethical conduct and honest governance.

The NBFCs that last aren’t always the fastest growing. They’re the ones whose compliance team has a seat at the strategy table.

What’s the one lesson you’d add? 👇

posts.title: Most sentiment signals are constructed from the wrong news sources.
posts.author: YUKKA
posts.snippet:
Most sentiment signals are constructed from the wrong news sources.

Every day, there are 2 million news pieces written, every piece of news potentially carrying important information about your investment’s next move. 

A new quant research paper from Yukka's internal research team puts a number on a problem practitioners have suspected for years: of ˜240,000 news sources carrying company-specific sentiment data, predictive content is concentrated in a core panel of ~36,000 sources with the highest explanatory power for equity returns.

Filtering to this panel across ~22,000 listed equities from 2015–2025, increases weighted mean IC from 0.006 to 0.041.

That's a 6.8x improvement in average signal quality, with no meaningful loss in company coverage.

The implication is direct: sentiment factors constructed from unfiltered news aggregation substantially understate the true information content available in the data. The signal was always there. The noise was in the way. And Yukka can help you find it. 

The filtering framework is source-level, not article-level; each source is evaluated by its time-series IC consistency (information ratio) scaled to a t-statistic over its full active history. 

This penalises sources with short track records and rewards those with persistent, stable cross-sectional predictability over extended periods. The result is a compact quality panel that covers the investable universe without the drag of low-signal sources diluting factor construction.

The full methodology — including the IC decay matrix, temporal stability analysis across four market regimes (2015–2025), and horizon-specific signal structure — is available in the white paper. 

Download it here: https://lnkd.in/dGX3bx46 

Source: Whitepaper Measuring Sentiment Decay — Quant Research, Yukka AG

posts.title: A question buyers in Beavercreek Township ask all the time: "I'm already paying for title insurance for the bank. Why would I buy a second policy?"
posts.author: Doug Haney
posts.snippet:
A question buyers in Beavercreek Township ask all the time: "I'm already paying for title insurance for the bank. Why would I buy a second policy?"

Here's the short version. If you finance, your lender will almost certainly require a lender's title policy. But that policy protects the lender's loan. It doesn't protect your down payment or your equity. Only an owner's policy does that, and it's optional.

Ohio's new title insurance rate schedule took effect January 1, 2026. Under it, a lender's policy issued at the same closing as an owner's policy drops to a small flat charge ($150 for a standard policy, $175 for an expanded one). So buying both together keeps the added cost of protecting yourself modest, and it's a one-time premium that can cover you for as long as you or your heirs own the home.

One more thing buyers don't always know: if you're using a federally related mortgage, the seller can't require you to use a particular title company. Federal law makes a seller who does that liable for three times the title charges. You get to shop, and you should compare bottom-line totals.

I wrote up the full breakdown, including a decision checklist and the 2026 Ohio rates side by side:
https://lnkd.in/gPVPCUGX

If you're buying anywhere in Greene County or within an hour of Springfield, I'm happy to walk through your closing decisions with you before you write an offer.

posts.title: Yesterday Dr Helen Haines, an independent MP, was critically injured outside her electorate office in what the PM has called a deliberate attack. A man has been arrested. His motiv
posts.author: Simone Herbert-Lowe
posts.snippet:
Yesterday Dr Helen Haines, an independent MP, was critically injured outside her electorate office in what the PM has called a deliberate attack. A man has been arrested. His motives are a matter for the police and, in due course, the courts. My thoughts are with Dr Haines and her family.

Whatever the facts turn out to be, no-one should have to consider their physical safety when standing for Parliament. When that becomes normal, fewer good people put their hand up, and we are all worse off.

As a woman, it's hard not to feel the world is becoming more dangerous. While there is no evidence to connect social media with this incident, it raises concerning issues, particularly given a national survey released last year found almost one in ten Australians agreed violence can sometimes be justified to advance a cause.

In June, ASIO’s Director-General said that “social media is amplifying and accelerating grievance narratives, eroding trust in institutions, promoting discord and inflammatory rhetoric, exacerbating polarisation and creating a permissive environment for violence.”

A handful of foreign tech companies now control the platforms where public debate happens, the networks that carry critical communications, and the AI models built into both.

X owner Elon Musk publicly called our eSafety Commissioner a “censorship commissar”. Ms Inman Grant has said that within 24 hours, 75,000 posts were directed at her, about 80% of them toxic or harmful, including death threats.

The sovereignty risk is real. This month Ukraine’s interceptor drones lost connectivity after a speed cap was applied to Starlink terminals. Who imposed it is disputed, but what isn’t is that a capability central to Ukraine’s defence was turned down from outside the country.

Musk’s AI company is suing Minnesota over its ban on tools that generate non-consensual sexual images, arguing the law burdens “the tools of visual expression”. A UK MP has gone to court to stop its Grok chatbot generating sexualised deepfakes of her. Women are overwhelmingly the targets of this abuse.

US law shields platforms from liability for user content, and there is now debate about whether that extends to generative AI. None of it was designed with Australian interests in mind, which is why we need our own rules.

The government has responded with the Online Safety Act, the social media minimum age and criminal offences for sharing deepfake sexual material. The remaining gap is accountability for design: how platforms amplify and recommend content. A legislated duty of care with meaningful penalties would help, as would a direct right of action that doesn’t carry prohibitive cost risk.

This has long been a country where MPs can walk down the street and meet constituents without fear. Are we comfortable with how much of our public debate is now shaped by a few tech owners based overseas?

💸The UK is about to spend £298 billion on defence over the next four years. 

Over the past few months we’ve interviewed founders, investors, industry bodies and former members of the Armed Forces about getting UK defence tech into service. 

The money and the rules have moved. The Procurement Act now gives suppliers sight of contracts up to 36 months ahead, and the MoD can award directly to SMEs.

Yet the founders described the same stall again and again. 

🔄The pilot works - the technology is proven - then long buying cycles, red tape and money sitting in the wrong budget hold it up for months, sometimes years. 
Several in the cohort have moved core operations to the US, Germany or Asia, where capital and contracts come sooner.

I’ve spent 20 years helping tech companies scale across markets, and I know how this plays out. When a home market is slow to buy, good companies grow somewhere else. In defence the cost is higher, because while proven kit waits, the risk sits with the people in service.
🗨️As Air Marshal Andrew Turner CB CBE put it to us: “Time is the biggest risk we face, and we just don’t have enough of it.”

Voices of Defence Tech: Inside the UK Procurement Gap, a white paper from Think & Grow sets out what’s already working and the practical steps founders, primes, investors and the MoD can take now.

posts.title: A vendor can't invoke a law that was never written into the contract to walk away from it. That's effectively what the Delhi High Court held last month, a dispute every legal team
posts.author: Nehha Sharma
posts.snippet:
A vendor can't invoke a law that was never written into the contract to walk away from it. That's effectively what the Delhi High Court held last month, a dispute every legal team managing SaaS and tech vendor contracts should be watching.

#SAP India suspended enterprise software support to #NayaraEnergy in July 2025, after the EU sanctioned #Nayara over its Rosneft ownership stake. SAP's defence was that its support function routes partly through its German parent, so continuing service would breach #EU sanctions law.

The contract between SAP India and Nayara, though, was governed by Indian law. The Court held SAP couldn't structure its own service delivery through an EU entity and then use that structure to claim Indian-law performance had become impossible. Unproven foreign sanctions, at the interim stage, weren't enough of a defence. SAP was ordered to restore services to the pre-suspension position and the matter continues, with the next hearing in November.

For anyone drafting #vendor or #SaaS agreements with multinational providers: a sanctions clause only protects a vendor if it's actually written into the contract, naming which regimes apply and what evidence triggers suspension. Silence on that point doesn't hand a vendor an exit. It hands them a #breach claim.

That clause needed negotiating before signature, not argued over in court after services went dark.

#ContractDrafting #SaaS #CrossBorderContracts #Legal #Corporate
posts.reason: Vendor contracts and cross-border sanctions clauses are useful for their deep tech and defence clients, but the focus on Indian law and SaaS rather than crypto/fintech or export control limits relevance to their core practice.

comments.text: This is a useful reminder that force majeure and sanctions clauses are creatures of contract, not statute: if the contract is silent on which regime applies and what evidence triggers suspension, a vendor is making a unilateral factual argument, not exercising a contractual right, and courts will treat it that way.
Did the Court engage at all with whether SAP's German-parent routing was a genuine operational dependency rather than a structure chosen after the fact to manufacture a sanctions defence?

We draft sanctions carve-outs into vendor and SaaS agreements for exactly this reason: naming the regimes and the evidentiary trigger up front is cheap, arguing impossibility after services go dark in front of a judge is not.

posts.title: JPM Coin on Ethereum breaks a pattern I wrote about in September: banks like HSBC and DBS keep tokenised deposits on their own ledgers and leave public chains to stablecoins. I was
posts.author: Rohit Malekar
posts.snippet:
JPM Coin on Ethereum breaks a pattern I wrote about in September: banks like HSBC and DBS keep tokenised deposits on their own ledgers and leave public chains to stablecoins. I was wrong to assume deposits needed a private ledger. 

A whitelist in the token contract ties a JPMorgan deposit to JPMorgan’s approved clients, on a chain anyone can read.That restriction is also its limit. Every transfer moves dollars between two of JPMorgan’s own clients, so it says little yet about settlement between banks. 

Money moving between banks finishes in central bank money, and in the markets I follow that runs on private systems. In India it is the RBI’s wholesale CBDC. In Singapore, banks net payments on Swift’s ledger and settle through existing systems. In Hong Kong it is the HKMA’s RTGS system.

Capital rules keep bank exposure to public chains small. By default Basel puts any token on a permissionless chain in Group 2, its bucket for crypto like bitcoin, where a bank can end up holding capital equal to the full exposure. 

Singapore’s proposed way out of Group 2 caps a local bank’s exposure at 2% of its Tier 1 capital. I expect Ethereum to carry one bank’s deposits at a time until a central bank puts its money, or a link to it, on a public chain.

One step at a time.
posts.reason: Substantive analysis of tokenized deposits, regulatory capital treatment, and settlement infrastructure—relevant to crypto and RWA legal strategy.

comments.text: Worth adding that the Group 2 capital treatment is precisely why we have not seen a public-chain equivalent for EU bank deposit tokens yet - under MiCAR an e-money token issued by a bank still triggers EMT reserve and redemption requirements that make permissionless settlement unattractive before a CBDC link exists.

Do you think Singapore's 2% Tier 1 cap approach gets picked up anywhere in the EU, or does the Basel Group 2 treatment just push European banks toward permissioned ledgers entirely and leave public chains to stablecoin issuers?

We see the same split playing out in token classification work - issuers want the optionality of a public chain but the moment you introduce bank-grade KYC whitelisting, you are halfway back to a private ledger in substance if not in form.

JPMorgan’s Quiet "Walled Garden" Strategy
News broke that JPMorgan has launched its tokenized dollar deposit, "JPM Coin," on the Ethereum mainnet (L1).
While crypto natives are celebrating this as a "victory for Web3 and DeFi" or the "mass adoption of public chains," the mega-bank's true strategy is far more calculated—and remarkably shrewd.
They didn't embrace the open, permissionless ethos of Web3.
Instead, they simply free-rode on Ethereum’s robust public infrastructure to build their own closed "Walled Garden."
Here is what is actually happening behind the scenes:
1. Strict Access Control via Smart Contracts
Through smart contract white-listing, transactions are strictly limited to institutional clients who have passed JPMorgan’s rigorous KYC/AML checks. The core Web3 principle of "permissionless access" is completely shut out.
2. Leveraging Public Infrastructure as a Cost-Effective Rail
The era of spending millions to build and maintain private, proprietary blockchains is over. JPMorgan is leveraging Ethereum—a globally secured, time-tested ledger—as a mere data layer, positioning itself to dominate the settlement network for Real World Assets (RWAs).
3. Sidelining Third-Party Stablecoins
By promoting its own "deposit tokens" rather than third-party stablecoins like USDT or USDC, JPMorgan eliminates issuer counterparty risk while locking in institutional liquidity, settlement fees, and client relationships.
The very technology originally designed to disintermediate banks is now being seamlessly weaponized by the world's largest bank to maximize its capital efficiency and solidify its grip on future financial infrastructure.
Behind the hype of crypto adoption lies a masterclass in TradFi's strategic cunning.
Is this the first decisive step toward TradFi completely taking over blockchain rails?

posts.title: Imagine a crypto token, backed by gold. Its issuer decides it belongs in the lightest category under Europe’s crypto rules, with no authorization and no strict reserve requirements
posts.author: Gama Glória

Imagine a crypto token, backed by gold. Its issuer decides it belongs in the lightest category under Europe’s crypto rules, with no authorization and no strict reserve requirements. Under MiCA, that is the issuer’s call. The token goes to market, and investors buy in. 

But what if a supervisor takes a closer look later, and disagrees? What are the stakes? Who's exposed to the risk? 

ESMA and EBA both call classification one of the hardest practical questions in the MiCA regime, and their responses to the EU’s review point in different directions. Read together, they suggest that they debate is moving toward a different question altogether, and it's a question of power: who decides?  

In the latest essay in our series GG Thinks, Afonso Almeida Luís unpacks the proposals and closes with four questions that every token issuer should be able to answer early. 

Read it in English and Portuguese on our website, via the link in the first comment.  

#gamagloria #lawforstrategists #MiCA #cryptoassets #tokenization

FINMA Approves Switzerland’s First Bitcoin ETF

FINMA has approved Switzerland’s first exchange-traded retail fund investing directly in Bitcoin, classified as an “other fund for alternative investments” with specific risks under Swiss law.

Given Bitcoin’s trading history and liquidity, FINMA has granted an exemption from the applicable risk diversification requirements. Investor protection is addressed through:
- Custody and operational safeguards to mitigate crypto-specific risks.
- FinSA conduct obligations, including risk disclosures and suitability assessments where applicable.
- Enhanced transparency regarding investment risks in the fund documentation.

FINMA emphasises that regulatory approval does not reduce Bitcoin’s inherent market risks, particularly its high volatility and potential for substantial losses. The approval follows FINMA’s 2021 authorisation of a crypto fund for qualified investors and marks a further step in providing regulated crypto investment products to Swiss retail investors.

posts.title: In March 2026, a G7 central bank rebuilt its model of the economy around the fact that households are different.
posts.author: gary hunt
posts.snippet:
In March 2026, a G7 central bank rebuilt its model of the economy around the fact that households are different.

Seven months before the Nobel Prize would canonise the microfoundations of macroeconomic stabilisation, the Bank of England published UK-HANK — a medium-scale Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian model, Macro Technical Paper No. 7.

Gone is the representative household. The model features rich household heterogeneity, housing and balance-sheet structures, and marginal propensities to consume calibrated to real UK evidence. The same interest-rate decision no longer acts on the household — it acts on a distribution of balance sheets and savings buffers. Monetary transmission has become a distributional question, and the Bank has built the machinery to see it.

The Bank of England takes that distribution as given — an input to be calibrated. Our work asks the prior question: what produces that distribution in the first place?

That is the question our same-month SSRN paper, The Household Affordability Frontier, was written to answer: structural costs form a frontier — the threshold at which costs exceed a households capacity to convert potential into capability. Below it, households optimise for survival; above it, they invest in learning, mobility and long-horizon decision-making. National productivity cannot sustainably outperform the underlying capacity of its households.

Two March 2026 documents. One measures the distribution. One explains what forms it.

Founded in 2020, Liquid Swords develops computer and console games and has built a highly skilled and diverse development team with experience from studios including DICE, Rockstar, Starbreeze and Avalanche Studios. comments.text: In a game studio bankruptcy sale the real diligence item is usually not the copyright in the code but whether engine licences, middleware and third-party IP assignments from contractors actually transfer cleanly to a buyer.

We do a fair amount of IP assignment and founder agreement work in gaming studios precisely because this kind of gap only surfaces at the worst possible moment, in a sale or insolvency process.

posts.title: Working together across borders is essential if we are to protect and strengthen the rights of audiovisual authors around the world. National and international organisations each b
posts.author: Barbara Hayes
posts.snippet:
Working together across borders is essential if we are to protect and strengthen the rights of audiovisual authors around the world. National and international organisations each bring valuable experience, expertise and relationships—and our collective voice is stronger when we use them together. That is why cooperation between national organisations like The Authors'​ Licensing & Collecting Society and European and international organisations like the Society of Audiovisual Authors (SAA), CISAC and AVACI matters so much. 

Particularly at the World Intellectual Property Organization – WIPO, joining forces helps us make the strongest possible case for authors’ rights and fair remuneration. National circumstances across the globe may differ, but we share a determination to ensure that the people behind the stories we watch are recognised, respected and properly rewarded.

I was very pleased to be invited to contribute to AVACI’s Annual Congress held this year in Japan. Although I was sorry not to be there in person, the miracles of technology allowed me to join in spirit—and on screen! Thank you to our colleagues for bringing us together and keeping these important conversations moving forward. With AI and changing markets presenting shared challenges, international cooperation has never mattered more.

posts.title: If you sell into health systems, you’ve almost certainly wished for a list of every hospital’s EHR and the exact version it runs. Yes, market research firms will sell you something
posts.author: Brendan Keeler
posts.snippet:
If you sell into health systems, you’ve almost certainly wished for a list of every hospital’s EHR and the exact version it runs. Yes, market research firms will sell you something that purports to solve that problem, but are you ready to drop those stacks and pray their answer isn’t some bullshit small sample size survey? If you're a startup, probably not, I imagine.

But hold up just one second! Here in healthcare, we are built different (thanks to unrivaled regulation)! Here, the answer sits in public - free and refreshed by federal law, just a few cURLs away. You have the ability to introspect the market for hyperprecise targeting along EHR lines (or even specific EHR version lines)! How we ended up with such a gift deserves a short detour.

Using that superpower on our nation's largest EHR to start, it turns out Epic sites really don’t have all that much version drift:
- Of the 457 distinct servers behind Epic’s Brands directory, 452 answered
- 95% run a release from the past year
- Only 23 run anything older, while the oldest is February 2025
- Between two runs a week apart, 47 servers upgraded.

Most of the laggards have a story:
- CommonSpirit’s legacy servers look frozen while it consolidates onto a single instance 
- Epic’s older R4 list still carries a few servers on releases from 2022 to 2024, but every one belongs to an organization that has already moved to a newer instance

Data is cool! All that and a how-to guide to follow along yourself in the article
